title: Linked 2D and 3D views: how do the views correspond?
summary: A top-down contour view and a 3D surface of the same function, with one shared selected point marked in both and its values quoted. It teaches you to follow a point between representations.

media.alt: Two linked views of the same function: a top-down contour map with a selected point and crosshairs, and a 3D surface with a dotted stem and a note giving the selection values.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

read_the_figure.question: How do the views correspond?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: x and y from -2 to 2, colour f (viridis). Right: the same x, y and f as a surface (f from about -0.5 to 1.2). A shared selection (x = 0.7, y = -0.5, f = 0.87) is marked with an amber dot and dotted guide lines.
look_at: Where is the selection in the 2D view and what colour is the field there?
Can you find the selection in the 3D view? Is the marker visible?
Does the height at the selection (0.87) match the colour on the contour map?
Which features line up: peaks, valleys, saddles?
read_the_figure.proves: The two views show the same function, and a shared selection ties a point in one to a point in the other. It does not prove the function is what the model claims; it only exposes its shape.
if_wrong: A selection that appears in one view but not the other.
Different colour scales in the two views: yellow means different values.
A 3D view whose surface hides the marker: the selection cannot be found, as in this render.

terms.meaning: Two or more views of the same data that update together when the reader selects or moves something.
A point, region or time chosen once and highlighted in every view.
The 2D map of a field seen from above, with colour for height.
The 3D plot where height is the third axis.
Dotted lines through the selection that read its coordinates on the axes.

remember: Same function, same colour map, same limits in both views.
Read coordinates from the crosshair, value from the quote.
3D hides: use the 2D view to locate and the 3D to understand shape.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: position in the plane encodes (x, y) and colour encodes f; the amber dot with dotted crosshairs marks the selection. Right: position in 3D encodes (x, y, f); the surface uses the same colour map. The amber boxed note states the selection values. A 3D static preview is labelled as such.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A 2D map is easy to read accurately but its third dimension is colour; a 3D surface shows height as a shape but occludes and distorts. Linking them lets the reader use each for what it is good at: locate in 2D and see the shape in 3D, with one selection tying the two.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Where is the selection and what is the value? At x = 0.7, y = -0.5 in the 2D view, in the green-yellow region next to the yellow peak at (0.9, 0); the quote says f = 0.87. Q2: Does the colour agree? The colour there is yellow-green, near the top of the colour range, and the maximum of the field is about 1.2 at the peak, so 0.87 is about 70 percent of the peak: consistent. Q3: Can you find it in 3D? Only as the short dotted stem on the front slope below the yellow ridge; the amber marker itself is hidden by the surface, so the 3D view fails to carry the selection and the 2D view must be used to find it.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Shared selection: the single point shown in both views and the note that quotes it. If the selection does not appear in both, the views are not linked, only placed side by side.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Perspective distorts the apparent size and hides points behind ridges: the selection dot is behind the surface in the 3D panel and only a short dotted stem is visible. The colour scale is the only link of height to colour; if different maps are used the two views disagree. A static preview shows one angle, whereas a real view lets the user rotate. The function shown is smooth by construction and says nothing about sampling noise.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Slices through the surface along x and y at the selected point (two small line plots) give exact values and have no occlusion. A wireframe or a contour on the 3D surface can show the structure. A table of values near the selection is exact.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the profiles through the selected point on the left and bottom edges of the 2D view, and draw the marker with depth testing disabled.

checks.q: What is shared between the two views?
checks.answer: The selected point, shown in both.

checks.q: The 2D view shows a dark blob at (-0.9, 0) and the 3D surface shows a pit. Are these the same feature?
checks.answer: Yes: dark purple is the lowest f, and the pit in 3D is the same minimum; the two views use the same colour map so low values are dark in both.
